item.title: Fossil fuel divide fractures consensus at climate talks in Antalya
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environment, Environmental Economics, Environmental Politics, Fossil Fuels, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, and United Nations
item.description:
- The UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended without consensus, with countries unable to agree on reaffirming the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels.
- The Antalya negotiations exposed a fundamental divide over climate justice, with developing countries demanding recognition of historical responsibility and predictable finance before being asked to shoulder greater costs.
- India challenged the attempt to set new global targets without addressing who had used up the carbon budget and who must pay for the transition.
item.content:encoded: The UN climate summit in Antalya in Türkiye ended in a deadlock after nations could not agree even to reaffirm a transition away from fossil fuels. Three days earlier, leaders of China, Russia and the U.S. declared that their countries planned to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. One meeting was a climate negotiation, the other a separate diplomatic gathering. But together they exposed a stark reality. While the climate crisis demands a rapid shift away from coal, oil and gas, some of the world’s most powerful nations remain committed to expanding petroleum supply. The failure in Antalya was more than a breakdown over the wording of a final statement. Eleven years after the Paris Agreement established the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C, governments could not agree on a political declaration that would have reaffirmed a commitment they had already made three years before in Dubai. The disagreement also exposed a deeper divide over who should pay for the transition and whether developing countries would receive the support needed to make it without sacrificing their people’s development and livelihoods. From Dubai to deadlock The retreat was visible in the successive drafts of the proposed Antalya Pact. The first version of the host’s proposed statement, released on November 16, reaffirmed the commitment made in Dubai in 2023 to move away from fossil fuels in energy systems and called for accelerated action to phase them out. item.title: The climate risks behind pumped-storage expansion
item.dc:creator: Lisann Dias
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Climate Change, Dams, Extreme Weather Events, Hydroelectric power, Impacts of Climate Change, Industry, Mountains, and Western Ghats
item.description:
- India aims to achieve installed pumped-storage capacity of 87 GW by 2034 and cross 100 GW by 2036.
- A roadmap released by the Central Electricity Authority identifies the Western Ghats region as having the highest potential for pumped-storage projects, with Maharashtra leading the country with many projects.
- Experts have raised concerns about the location of proposed projects in the Western Ghats, calling for climate-risk assessments and studies that consider the cumulative impact of multiple projects.
item.content:encoded: In June 2005, heavy rainfall triggered a landslide at the site of Maharashtra’s Ghatghar pumped-storage project, then under construction in Thane district. Water, rocks and debris rapidly flowed into the project’s tailrace tunnel, trapping nearly 22 workers. Nearly two decades later, as India seeks to expand renewable energy and build storage capacity, the country is pushing for pumped-storage projects or PSPs in the same region. PSPs are a kind of “water battery” that uses surplus electricity to pump water uphill into a reservoir, storing that energy as elevated water. The water is released downhill to a lower reservoir to generate power. According to a roadmap released by the Central Electricity Authority in January, India’s total installed PSP capacity is expected to reach 87 GW by 2034 and cross 100 GW by 2036, with an average annual addition of 9 GW. The report identifies the western region as having the highest PSP potential, with Maharashtra leading both the region and the country with 56,355 MW. “As the grid becomes renewable-heavy, pumped storage serves as a viable long-duration storage technology,” explains Disha Aggarwal, fellow at the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), a New Delhi-based think tank. “It becomes important in managing fluctuations in electricity supply and demand across days and seasons, and to meet unexpected shortfalls.” In Maharashtra, 400 MW is already operational, 2500 MW is under construction, 6,300 MW has been approved by the CEA but is yet to be taken up for construction, and 24,800 MW is at…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Why deforestation science gets shifting cultivation wrong [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Amit John Kurien
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Commentary, Conservation, Deforestation, Ecology, Forests, Habitat Loss, Indigenous Peoples, Land Rights, Natural Resources, Research, and Tribes
item.description:
- Some studies on the drivers of global deforestation inaccurately attribute forest loss to shifting cultivation.
- Confusing tree cover with forests, and land cover with land use distorts both the estimates of forest as well as causes of deforestation.
- Flawed map classifications have real-world consequences. For shifting cultivation landscapes, it can harm livelihoods of millions of upland tribes who rely on it for food security and nutrition.
- The views in the commentary are that of the author.
item.content:encoded: Estimating deforestation — the permanent conversion of forest to another land use — is only as reliable as our ability to distinguish one land use from another. If we get that wrong, we misjudge not only how much forest is being lost but also what is driving the loss. Consider shifting cultivation, also known as swidden farming. This rotational mountain agriculture of the tropical world was considered and continues to be portrayed in international policy and academic literature as one of the leading causes of deforestation. A misunderstood land use, it was vilified as ‘backward’ and ‘primitive’ from colonial times across the tropical upland regions from South America to Africa and South and Southeast Asia. To make things worse, the Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) made a global appeal in 1957, wrongly blaming shifting cultivation as the “greatest obstacle” to “conservation of production potential… of soil and forests”. This narrative only deepened the anti-shifting cultivation stance among post-colonial nations. They sought to settle shifting cultivators in the hills and mountains worldwide for ease of taxation and administration. Today, it survives regardless, playing a vital role for food security among marginal farmers in places with little mainstream market access. Many academic studies and national forest surveys blame shifting cultivation for deforestation without actually measuring its extent. item.title: Forest villagers protest tourism curbs after tiger translocation
item.dc:creator: Nabarun Guha
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Activism, Big Cats, Biodiversity, Conservation, Forests, Human Rights, Mammals, National Parks, Protected Areas, Tigers, Tourism, Villages, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Buxa Tiger Reserve’s tiger reintroduction programme began with the translocation of T138 from Bihar’s Valmiki Tiger Reserve.
- Forest villagers protested restrictions on tourism activities imposed to minimise disturbance and allow the tigress to acclimatise.
- The tiger recovery programme, planned over a decade ago, involved habitat restoration and prey-base improvement.
item.content:encoded: A three year old tigress, T138 was released in Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal on October 2. While the translocation has been lauded as an important step in wildlife conservation, people living in forest villages have protested restrictions on tourism activities imposed to minimise disturbance and allow the tigress to acclimatise. The translocation was the result of a joint initiative of the West Bengal Forest Department and National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA). The tigress which was brought from the Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar was soft released into an enclosure on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti. Two days later, it reportedly stepped out of the enclosure and walked into the wild. Bhupender Yadav, Union Cabinet Minister for Forest, Environment and Climate Change celebrated the tiger reintroduction to Buxa on his social media. Why Buxa, declared a tiger reserve in 1983 under Project Tiger, needed a translocated tiger to repopulate it, points to decades of poaching, habitat degradation, poor prey base and biotic pressures, among others that wiped out the apex predators from the landscape. All India tiger estimation in 2018 recorded no tigers in Buxa which continued until late 2021 when camera traps showed one male tiger. Chief Wildlife Warden of West Bengal, Pradeep Vyas shared that the gradual disappearance of tigers in Buxa Tiger Reserve (BTR) started from 1970 onwards. “I think tigers mainly disappeared due to biotic interference in the park and poaching of their prey base. item.title: Global electrification push meets resistance over money and fairness
item.dc:creator: Kundan Pandey
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Energy, and Villages
item.description:
- COP31 presidency aims to build consensus among parties on its flagship agenda to raise electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035.
- There is consensus that electricity wastes far less energy than burning fuel; however, developing countries oppose any binding commitment related to electricity.
- India is pushing electrification to cut imports and pollution. It has raised the issue of finance, a constraint in mitigation efforts.
item.content:encoded: The UN climate summit in Türkiye’s Antalya has been pushing an ambitious global goal of raising electricity’s share of total final energy use to 35% by 2035. However, the latest draft suggests the final outcome may be weaker. The second and latest draft of the COP31 cover decision, the summit’s main political text, was released on November 19. It calls for increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35% globally by 2035, complementary to efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally. But the language is softer than in the first draft. The first draft, which appeared on November 16, had a separate paragraph on the electrification goal. It called on countries to contribute “in a nationally determined manner.” In the new draft, the target is no longer a call on countries to contribute. It is listed as one of the “concrete solutions” for “global cooperation across all actors”, placed alongside the existing global pledge to triple renewable energy capacity. The softer wording follows resistance to the first draft from several negotiating blocs. The Like-Minded Developing Countries, a negotiating bloc of around two dozen countries including India, China and Bangladesh, said they would not support any recognition of the pledge in the text. The Arab Group and Russia also rejected the draft text over its language on fossil fuels and the electrification goal. Further revisions are actively being negotiated on the second draft, ahead of the summit’s scheduled close on November 20. item.title: El Niño could deepen Tamil Nadu’s water stress and threaten agriculture
item.dc:creator: Krithiga Narayanan
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Science, Drought, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Monsoons, Villages, and Water
item.description:
- Tamil Nadu’s existing climate stress could intensify due to El Niño, increasing the risks of drought as well extreme rainfall.
- Uneven monsoon rainfall and decreasing groundwater resources are making agricultural systems more vulnerable.
- With the El Niño likely to strengthen, experts call for disaster preparedness, effective water management and climate-resilient farming to mitigate its potential impacts.
item.content:encoded: Climate change induced global warming is significantly increasing baseline ocean temperatures and worsening the impacts of the naturally occurring El Niño cycle. The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) recently confirmed an 80-100% probability of the persistent El Niño phase extending to April 2027. For regions like India which are already climate stressed, this El Niño can have a multiplier effect, exacerbating existing vulnerabilities. India experienced 16 El Niño events between 1951 and 2025 and they last generally for nine to 18 months. This year’s El Niño is projected to be severe and its impacts can already be seen in the form of extreme droughts or excess rainfall. The southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu is staring at an acute water stress as it is already impacted on various fronts due to climate change. According to a 52-year climate study conducted between 1971 and 2022 published in International Journal of Climatology, the south peninsular region of India, including Tamil Nadu, is prone to drought. The study highlights that Tamil Nadu’s drought risk is a long-term trend. Tamil Nadu depends on inflows from the southwest monsoon to replenish its reservoirs and rainfall from the northeast monsoon season for its water security. The southwest monsoon occurs between June and September and the northeast monsoon occurs between October and December. El Niño has the potential to influence rainfall including the northeast monsoon. item.title: The world struggles to pay for the growing human cost of climate change
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environment, Environmental Politics, Extreme Weather Events, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Pollution, and United Nations
item.description:
- The international response to climate losses remains inadequate, leaving vulnerable communities to bear the costs of damage they did little to cause.
- The loss and damage fund has attracted pledges worth hundreds of millions of dollars, yet the money available is a fraction of what vulnerable countries need.
- From South Asia to the Pacific, affected communities face mounting losses that money alone cannot repair, while slow decisions and limited access leave many without meaningful support.
item.content:encoded: In 2022, floodwater engulfed the farm and home of Abdul Khalique Laghari, a farmer from Pakistan’s Sindh province. The water rose six to eight feet in some places. The crops were destroyed, houses were inundated and the land was left damaged. Four years later, farmers in the region are still struggling to cultivate it. “Our farms were underwater. The water entered our houses. Everything was destroyed,” Laghari said. He and more than 30 other farmers from Sindh are now seeking compensation for their losses. Their experience shows how climate damage reaches far beyond the moment a disaster strikes. A farmer loses not just a crop, but the income needed to feed a family and pay off debt. A coastal household may find its drinking water contaminated by salt. A fishing community may see its catch decline as the sea changes. An island community may face the loss of the land on which its history and identity are rooted. These are the human costs of climate change, increasingly recognised in international negotiations as loss and damage. They include the destruction caused by floods, storms and heatwaves, but also the slower damage from rising seas, coastal erosion and saltwater intrusion. Some losses can be repaired with money. Others are irreversible. The scale of the problem is growing. The World Meteorological Organization’s climate update, released as the annual UN climate summit in Türkiye’s Antalya opened, says the past 12 years are set to be the warmest on record. item.title: How an unfit boat design left Kerala’s fishers in debt
item.dc:creator: RoeqinSupriya Vohra
item.author: Kartik Chandramouli
item.topic-tags: Coast, Fish, Fishing, and Oceans
item.description:
- Kerala was the first state to receive deep-sea fishing vessels under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana. But boats designed without fishers’ input came with flaws that made them expensive to operate.
- Through the stories of Joseph, Shaju, Peter and other fishers, this illustrated story explores how a promise of better livelihoods turned into a struggle with debt. The story is second in a series on deep-sea fishing in India, produced with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network.
item.content:encoded: Joseph had purchased a deep-sea fishing vessel under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY), a central government scheme launched in 2020 that aims to convert traditional fishers into deep-sea fishers. He is from one of the 222 coastal fishing villages along Kerala’s 590 km coastline in south-west India. Fisheries is a major contributor to the state’s economy. It was the first state to receive deep-sea fishing vessels under the PMMSY. In the first year, Kerala spent about 12% of the total PMMSY budget, about ₹12 crores (₹120 million), on manufacturing ten deep-sea fishing boats. The boats were initially priced at ₹1.2 crore (₹12 million) each, but the cost rose to ₹1.5 crore (₹15 million) within three months of the scheme’s launch. Beneficiaries, mostly small-scale, generational coastal fishers who fished daily, were to contribute ₹72 lakhs (₹7.2 million) per boat, while the central and state governments would cover the rest. The state encouraged fisheries cooperatives to apply in groups of ten. It also helped them take three-year loans from the Kerala Finance Corporation to buy the boats. Eventually, the state selected six cooperative societies as beneficiaries, and six of the ten boats were sold. The Central Institute of Fisheries Technology, a national fisheries research institute, designed the boats, and Udupi Cochin Shipyard Ltd, a subsidiary of Cochin Shipyard Ltd., India’s largest shipbuilding and maintenance facility, manufactured them. With these deep-sea fishing boats, fishers were expected to be at sea for at least 20 days at a time, navigating choppy waters…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: The fragility of mountains loom large over COP31
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environmental Politics, Extreme Weather Events, Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, Glaciers, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Himalayas, Impacts of Climate Change, and Mountains
item.description:
- Nepal and Bhutan’s bid for a standalone agenda on the vulnerability of mountains to climate change was edged out of the COP31, but these concerns still made it into the draft cover text.
- With overshoot of 1.5°C near certain, experts warns that cryosphere losses are irreversible on human timescales, and only 16% of Himalayan glaciers may survive the century at current emission levels.
- Some Parties fear added costs and obligations, and several major countries, including India, did not attend the high level segment on mountains at the summit.
item.content:encoded: The proposal to include an agenda item focussed on the impacts of rising temperatures on high mountain ranges may have been rejected at the ongoing COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, but that hasn’t stopped the talks from spotlighting their catastrophic impacts — and the urgent need to address them. A special update by the World Meteorological Organisation estimates the Earth lost 400 gigatonnes of glacier ice in 2025. The push for a stand-alone item dedicated to warming in the mountains was championed by Nepal, which in August suffered devastating flash floods caused by a rock-ice avalanche, along with Bhutan and Kyrgyzstan. The vulnerability of the high mountain ranges has been “underrepresented within the core decision-making tracks of the UNFCCC,” Nepal argued in its submission, adding that the COP31 provided an opportunity to integrate “mountain-specific priorities into adaptation, finance and loss-and-damage frameworks.” Though the proposal was ultimately inched out of the formal agenda by competing interests — including a flagship proposal for electrification — its concerns are echoed in the COP31’s draft cover text, a strategic document summarising the summit’s priority areas, released on November 16. “When the standalone agenda item, co-proposed with Bhutan, was not adopted, Nepal pivoted swiftly to mainstream cryosphere and mountain priorities across existing negotiating tracks. That diplomatic pivot is yielding concrete results,” Lila Pieters Yahia, Nepal’s UN Resident Coordinator, told Mongabay-India over email. item.title: The secretive salamanders of the Himalayas
item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Aditi Tandon

Every monsoon in Darjeeling, the Himalayan salamander emerges from the forest floor to breed in small ponds known locally as pokhris. Males and females engage in a delicate courtship dance, after which fertilised eggs are laid on half-submerged vegetation. The larvae hatch into the water […]
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. Every monsoon in Darjeeling, the Himalayan salamander emerges from the forest floor to breed in small ponds known locally as pokhris. Males and females engage in a delicate courtship dance, after which fertilised eggs are laid on half-submerged vegetation. The larvae hatch into the water over the next two weeks, then develop lungs and adopt a terrestrial lifestyle. Once sexually mature, they return to their birth ponds to breed. There are about 830 species of salamanders worldwide, predominantly found in North America, Europe, and Asia. India hosts only two species. The Himalayan salamander (Tylototriton himalayanus), also called the Himalayan crocodile newt, is found in eastern Nepal, the Darjeeling Himalayas, and western Bhutan. It has a brown body with a blunt snout and rows of knobby warts along its back that may release toxins when disturbed. Adults are found near water bodies from roughly late April to early October. They spend the rest of the year on land, hiding under rocks or logs. The Manipuri newt (Tylototriton zaimeng), also known as the Zaimeng newt, was described only in 2023. It has a broad head, a rounded snout and short limbs. Its brown skin carries orange-yellow markings on the head, back, and sides, and on the palms and soles. It is restricted to the Khongtheng mountain range, Manipur, where it was first found at Zaimeng lake and in surrounding mountain lakes and ponds. item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Kartik Chandramouli
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Biodiversity, Human Wildlife Conflict, and Wildlife
item.description: On the shifting sandbars of the Teesta in West Bengal, migrant farmers cultivate seasonal crops that are increasingly attracting elephants from nearby forests. The elephants feed on these crops, bringing people and wildlife into close contact. As the Teesta changes course, floods and erosion reshape the sandbars, forcing farmers to move their fields and adapt […]
item.content:encoded: On the shifting sandbars of the Teesta in West Bengal, migrant farmers cultivate seasonal crops that are increasingly attracting elephants from nearby forests. The elephants feed on these crops, bringing people and wildlife into close contact. As the Teesta changes course, floods and erosion reshape the sandbars, forcing farmers to move their fields and adapt to the changing landscape. Elephants, meanwhile, follow the seasonal crops and return to the sandbars to feed. Farmers lose crops, see elephants damage their homes and spend sleepless nights guarding their fields. Yet, despite years of living alongside elephants, they receive no formal compensation for crop losses.This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Institutional campuses could expand India’s conservation network, but challenges remain
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Sreekandan
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Cities and Towns, Conservation, Ecology, Ecosystem services, Environment, Plants, Sustainability, and Trees
item.description:
- As India chases biodiversity targets, some researchers propose considering long-protected institutional campuses as Other Effective area-based Conservation Measure (OECM) sites, adding to the country’s protected area network.
- A case study of the CSIR-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute in Nagpur, Maharashtra, showcases the campus as a biodiversity reservoir and an ecological link in an urban environment.
- At the same time, experts urge caution, citing the lack of statutory backing for OECMs and the need for sustained management of campuses to secure their long-term conservation.
item.content:encoded: At the 2022 United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15), world governments, including India, adopted the historic Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, whereby signatories agreed to protect and conserve at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas, and oceans by 2030. According to a recent analysis, India’s protected area network covers roughly 28% of its geographical area through various regulatory frameworks: protected areas under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972; forest lands classified under the Indian Forest Act, 1927; and biodiversity heritage sites declared under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. While that estimate is close to the 30% target for 2030, India can bridge the remaining 2% only through shared spaces and not spared spaces (national parks and sanctuaries), said Jagdish Krishnaswamy, the dean of the School of Environment and Sustainability at the Indian Institute for Human Settlements, Bengaluru. Other Effective area-based Conservation Measure (OECM) is a novel conservation instrument that falls under shared spaces. Krishnaswamy defines OECM sites as “any land or waterscape that is not part of the protected area system, but where biodiversity is a core benefit simply because of the way that area is managed”. In 2022, India formally declared the Aravalli Biodiversity Park in Haryana as its first OECM site. In a document prepared by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), the National Biodiversity Authority of India (NBA), and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), 13 more sites across the country were identified and mapped as “potential OECMs”. item.title: Motherhood changes how sloth bears use forests in central India
item.dc:creator: Ananya Singh
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Animal Behaviour, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Forests, Mammals, National Parks, Protected Areas, Research, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Based on camera-trap surveys in Panna Tiger Reserve, a new study provides the first evidence of how female sloth bears with offspring and lone adults use the habitat differently.
- While lone adults preferred cooler, mixed forests, females with offspring occupied hotter, rugged terrain, and also showed greater daytime activity, possibly to avoid resource competition or potential infanticide.
- Researchers say occupying hotter, potentially less favourable areas may come at a physiological cost to sloth bear mothers.
item.content:encoded: Sloth bear mothers go weeks without food or water while nursing their young in caves or rocky crevices, eventually emerging from their maternal dens with cubs clinging to their backs. But how reproduction shapes their behavioural patterns remains poorly understood. A new study finds differences in how female sloth bears with offspring and lone adults in the forests of central India, use the habitat based on their needs. For this study published in Ecology and Evolution, researchers analysed camera-trap data from over 47,800 trap nights, collected over six seasons (two summers and four winters) between 2018 and 2021 in Panna Tiger Reserve, Madhya Pradesh. They found that while lone adults preferred mixed forest landscapes and cooler habitats, females with offspring occupied hotter, more rugged terrain and areas used less frequently by lone adults. “Space-wise, they (females with offspring) are actually avoiding lone adults very distinctly,” said Sankarshan Chaudhuri, a project scientist at the Wildlife Institute of India and the study’s lead author. He added that the consistent use of hotter areas by sloth bear mothers may impose physiological costs. “They are also adjusting their activity patterns with respect to the activity pattern of lone adults,” explained Chaudhuri. Although sloth bears are largely nocturnal and most active between dusk and dawn, females with offspring showed slightly greater daytime activity across seasons. “There is a fine-scale [temporal] segregation, which we didn’t expect,” Chaudhuri said. Researchers hypothesise that females with offspring may segregate to reduce competition for resources or to protect their cubs…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Türkiye climate summit’s finance gap threatens its promise of action
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Activism, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environment, Fossil Fuels, and Industry
item.description:
- Discussions and announcements in the first week of the annual UN climate summit in Antalya have exposed the gap between ambitious climate promises and the money needed to put them into practice.
- New initiatives proposed by hosts Türkiye and Australia may help countries prepare projects, but they cannot replace the predictable public finance that developing nations and emerging economies need.
- As negotiations enter their second and final week, disagreements over finance and the transition away from fossil fuels threaten to derail the summit’s promise of action.
item.content:encoded: Halfway through the annual United Nations climate summit being held in Türkiye’s Antalya, nearly 200 governments face the familiar question of where is the money to turn their promises into action? The meeting was billed as a turning point, a chance to move beyond pledges and start delivering results. However, as ministers prepare to take over negotiations in the second week, the central obstacle that has frustrated climate talks for years remains unresolved. Developing countries need far more money to protect their people from climate change and shift to cleaner energy. Developed countries have yet to agree on how much they will provide, in what form and when. UN Secretary-General António Guterres captured the scale of the crisis at the leaders’ summit on November 11. “The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” he said. Global emissions reached a record in 2025, and the world is certain to exceed the 1.5°C warming limit set out by the legally binding Paris Agreement in 2015. But the scale and duration of that overshoot can still be limited through faster action, Guterres said. That action will cost money. It means cleaner electricity, safer roads and buildings, better water systems, protection for farms and coastal communities, and early warnings that can save lives. Yet the countries most exposed to climate impacts often have the least money to prepare for them. The first week in Antalya has produced new initiatives and political promises. It has not produced a breakthrough on finance. That…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Climate movement takes its fight beyond emissions at Türkiye summit
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Activism, Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Environment, Forests, Fossil Fuels, Indigenous Rights, Pollution, and United Nations
item.description:
- Thousands of activists, workers and indigenous groups took to Antalya’s streets, turning a rainy day into a vibrant demonstration for climate justice during the ongoing climate conference.
- The protesters challenged fossil fuel dependence, corporate control of natural resources, forest destruction and the growing inequalities of climate change.
- Their demands went beyond emissions cuts to call for public control of energy, workers’ rights, climate finance and accountability for polluters.
item.content:encoded: A grey, rain-soaked day in Antalya in Türkiye burst into a riot of colour, music and slogans on November 14, when civil society called for a global day of action, held alongside COP31, the ongoing UN climate conference. Bright flags, hand-painted banners, giant street installations and costumed performers filled the city centre as thousands of climate activists, trade unionists and civil society campaigners marched through the streets. The rain did little to dampen their enthusiasm. Chants rang out against fossil fuels, corporate greed, forest destruction and economic injustice. The procession offered a striking contrast to the air-conditioned and sterile negotiating rooms of the international climate talks taking place in the city. Inside, government representatives were engaged in painstaking negotiations over finance, emissions and national commitments. Outside, people from different countries and movements were making their demands heard in a more direct and colourful manner. Their message was that climate change cannot be addressed simply by reducing emissions. It also requires confronting the economic interests and political choices that drive environmental destruction and inequality. The march opened the People’s Climate Summit, a parallel gathering held from November 14 to 18. More than 130 organisations are to be involved in around 150 events, with participants from 34 countries, according to its organisers. The procession on November 14 brought together movements working on issues ranging from fossil fuels and forest protection to workers’ rights, food systems, gender equality and peace. item.title: Three years on, Teesta’s flood survivors live in limbo as the river creeps closer

item.description:
- Nearly three years after the October 2023 glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) on Teesta river, displaced families still live in makeshift relief camps in Kalimpong, West Bengal, while those whose homes survived face a river that now sits closer and floods again each monsoon.
- Residents say there was no working early-warning system the night of the flood, and repeated surveys of damage have yet to produce housing, with 116 planned houses still awaiting state finance sanction.
- Sikkim sanctioned 4,100 houses and rental aid for those affected by the GLOF, but West Bengal never declared the flood a disaster and offered no housing scheme, leaving survivors in fear of eviction.
item.content:encoded: “When the flood took everything from me, it took more than my home and livelihood, it took away the place I once had in society. People look at us differently now. The relationships and respect we once had are no longer the same. I am not a beggar, and I was never born into a life like this.” Bijay Pradhan, 36, speaks about a loss that goes beyond a house. Before October 2023, when a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) surged through the Teesta river, his family had a home of their own and relied partly on agriculture and livestock rearing. After the flood, he became a daily-wage labourer supporting his mother, wife and two children. The family now lives in a temporary relief camp in Teesta Bazaar in Kalimpong, West Bengal, alongside hundreds of others. For him, losing the house also meant losing independence and social standing. The 2023 GLOF was caused by a breach of the South Lhonak Lake in upstream Sikkim, impacting 80,000 people. A 2025 study published in Science estimated that 270 million cubic metres of sediment were swept downstream by the flood. In Kalimpong, the Teesta riverbed reportedly rose between six and 14 metres, a central government committee tasked with documenting the river’s changed morphology found. Nearly three years after the flood, people are still rebuilding their lives on unstable land, with the possibility of another flood lingering each monsoon. item.title: Geopolitical shocks put energy security and clean energy transition in focus
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Carbon Finance, Cities and Towns, Clean Energy, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Coal, Energy, Environment, Environmental Economics, Fossil Fuels, Global Warming, Green Energy, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Industry, and Renewable Energy
item.description:
- Geopolitical shocks have made domestic clean energy a strategic necessity, but temporary falls in fossil fuel use will not deliver lasting emissions cuts.
- India must move beyond adding renewable capacity to displacing fossil fuels across its economy. Its ethanol programme shows how pursuing energy independence can create new pressures on land, water and food.
- Developing countries need affordable finance and technology to transition without bearing an unfair share of the costs.
item.content:encoded: The wars disrupting global energy markets have exposed the strategic weakness of an economy built on fossil fuels. Countries dependent on imported oil and gas can find their growth, public finances and energy supplies hostage to conflicts thousands of kilometres away. A threatened shipping route or an interruption in supplies can quickly raise the cost of transport, electricity and food. For India and much of the developing world, this is not an occasional inconvenience. It is a structural vulnerability. The case for domestic clean energy has never been stronger. Solar and wind power do not have to pass through contested shipping routes, and once installed, they provide electricity without the recurring cost of importing fuel. Electrifying transport and industry can reduce dependence on oil and gas. The transition is no longer simply an obligation born out of the climate crisis. It is now an economic and a strategic necessity. But there is a distinction that governments cannot afford to overlook. Energy security is not the same as a just transition. A country can reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels while creating new dependencies on critical minerals, intensifying competition for farmland and water, or leaving consumers with unreliable and unaffordable power. Developing countries face the harder task of building clean energy systems while coping with high borrowing costs, limited access to technology and far fewer financial resources than wealthy economies. item.title: No land to call their own, migrants and elephants coexist on a transient landscape
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Biodiversity, Conservation, Elephants, Habitat Fragmentation, Himalayas, Human Wildlife Conflict, Land Rights, Mammals, Migration, Rivers, Villages, Water, and Wildlife
item.description:
- In a charland on the Teesta in West Bengal, the lives and livelihoods, shaped by a constantly shifting landscape, are increasingly threatened by climate change.
- Although charlands support agriculture and provide refuge to landless migrants, residents face insecure land rights and precarious livelihoods.
- Elephants are increasingly using cultivated charlands as feeding grounds, adding to the challenges faced by residents.
- Human-elephant coexistence depends on understanding the wider landscape, including changing river systems, fragmented forests and expanding agriculture.
item.content:encoded: Fifty-seven-year-old Budharu Muhammed recalls a time when bombs, shells and ammunition flowed down the Teesta towards Premganj char, a sandbar settlement around 15 km from Jalpaiguri town in West Bengal. It was 2023, when a massive glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) from South Lhonak Lake in the Sikkim Himalayas caused a major surge in the Teesta, damaging infrastructure and affecting hydropower projects downstream. Silt, sand and rubble were flushed downstream. According to Muhammed, some army camps were flooded, explaining the sudden appearance of military materiel in his village and the panic it triggered. “There were other toxic things flowing down from medical shops and factories, oil from vehicles and gas cylinders. The water was murky with a layer of oil on top,” he says. People complained of skin rashes and itching after coming into contact with the water, he recalls, describing a time of uncertainty and fear. Located under Paharpur Gram Panchayat in the Sadar block of Jalpaiguri district, Premganj char, also known as Jaliapara, is identified as a highly vulnerable charland in the district’s disaster management plans. Adding to the woes of residents facing constant flooding and erosion is another threat: the movement of maljurians, or groups of male elephants. Maljurians comprise younger males and experienced adults that explore new landscapes, largely in search of food, explains Avijan Saha, a researcher with the wildlife conservation non-profit Airavat Trust who has studied the landscape for over a decade. “Other elephants can then follow the routes they have explored. item.title: Wildlife trade discourse overlooks trade in plants and other natural resources [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Lokesh MamThangsoi M. KhiamniunganUttara Mendiratta
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Commentary, Community based conservation, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Environmental Law, Forests, Insects, Plants, Wildlife Protection Act, Wildlife Trade, and Wildlife Trafficking
item.description:
- Wild plant trafficking remains largely overlooked, despite over 20% of assessed plant species being threatened with extinction.
- Unregulated trade extends beyond medicinal plants to orchids, mushrooms, insects and wildlife products, creating ecological and social consequences.
- Community-led monitoring and protection are crucial to conservation, alongside policies that recognise local livelihoods and support sustainable trade.
- The views in the commentary are that of the authors.
item.content:encoded: A simple question during a panel discussion on illegal wildlife trade at the Indian Wildlife Ecology Conference (IWEC) in 2024 got us thinking: What about plants and its trade? The panel admitted to the prevailing problem of “plant blindness”. While illegal wildlife trade brings to mind trafficking of orangutans, parrots, elephant ivory, and other endangered wildlife, there is rarely any conversation around plants. Except for the trade in high-value timber and ornamental plants, which have received some attention in the public eye, the trade in plants goes on largely unacknowledged. Over 20% of all plant species assessed by the IUCN Red List are threatened with extinction — a comparable level of extinction risk to mammals. And like the trade in wild animals, the trade in wild plants has serious and urgent conservation implications for species and ecosystems. Many researchers have highlighted the problem of large-scale extraction of threatened medicinal plants, which are often illegally laundered into legal markets. The collection happens across wide geographical expanses and involves local residents. The legal and conservation implications of this collection are not often apparent to local residents, nor is this considered a priority for enforcement agencies. As a result, the trade goes on, underreported and unaddressed. For many species, researchers acknowledge that local extinctions could happen without being recorded. A forest in Nagaland. While the topic of illegal wildlife trade brings to mind many endangered mammals, there is rarely any conversation around plants. item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. A recent study of Kerala’s Vypin-Kadamakkudy barrier island system recorded 20,927 dung beetles from 29 species, far more diversity than researchers expected in such an urbanising landscape. Dung beetles are scarab beetles, mostly of the subfamily Scarabaeinae, that feed, breed and nest in animal dung. Encased in a hard exoskeleton, they are also remarkably strong. The male horned dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus), for example, can pull up to 1,141 times its own body weight; equivalent to an average human adult lifting six double-decker buses. Dung beetles occur in forests, grasslands and deserts on every continent except Antarctica. They are vital ecological engineers, as they recycle animal waste, which in turn helps reduce methane emissions, aerate soil, and suppress pest flies. They are also secondary seed dispersers. There are more than 6,000 species of dung beetles worldwide, of which about 400-500 have been recorded in India. They are grouped by how they handle dung — rollers, such as Gymnopleurus species, shape it into balls and roll them away to bury elsewhere; tunnellers, such as Onitis species, dig chambers beneath the pat and bury it; and dwellers, such as Oniticellus species, breed inside the pat itself. They also differ in what they eat. Some species are generalists, surviving on the dung of any animal, while others are specialists, such as Heliocopris dominus, which can survive only on wild elephant dung.
